items.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: And the engineer was George Massenburg, who is my longest friend in the business, 50 years now.

ctx.x: Well you’ve got quite a lengthy resume and we’re not going to get through all of it, but I wanted to talk first about session musicians. I’ve been lucky to interview some fairly well known producers, a fellow named Joel Dorn, George Avakian. They were not — they didn’t play instruments. And I’m wondering if your own, being a guitarist and starting out as a session musician has informed your production choices and skills.

Well it helped me but I can tell you many producers, who are not musicians or were not musicians, Rick Hall in Muscle Shoals, Alabama could play but he wasn’t a great musician, but he was a great producer. I’ve known him, like I say if you talk to ten of us, how we got into it, you’ll get ten different stories. I actually didn’t start as a session player. I came from Richmond, Virginia, and when I was 14 we started a band, some friends, we started a little five piece band because of the Beatles. But by the time I…

of Richmond on Monday morning. So everybody went back but me. He said, “Do you want to stay over and watch me mix tomorrow? Monday morning. I said yeah. So I stayed over, go to the studio on Monday morning and we’re in one studio, in Baltimore and this was of course four track recording. And in another studio across the hall I saw these guys walking in with guitar cases and stuff, I said, “Who are they?” He said, “They’re studio musicians.” He said they’re here to play on somebody’s record or a jingle or…

items.title: Buckingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2019
items.q: But George and I would go from Baltimore where he had a studio, a four track, we’d go to Philadelphia, Sigma Sound, ‘cause they had an eight track.

ctx.x: Yeah. That’s why I wondered about better.

No, this morning in the class, this jazz class this morning, I was talking about recording. And I said when I started recording it was on 4-track. These guys were doing mono of course on disk and even when tape started it was mono. And then 2-track and eventually 3-track, then 4-track. I started in ’69 on 4-track, and then we’d go to Philadelphia, George Massenburg, my oldest friend in the business who is the man. He invented parametric equalization and all this stuff. We’re still friends. But George and I would…

Well that’s why when I listen to the Basie, they call it the All American Rhythm Section, it just sounds like one entity. Because they, I don’t know if they were so totally conscious of balancing their own volume but they surely did. And I had the experience once, on multiple, this one night after the other at a festival I heard the L.A. Juggernaut Big Band, Frankie Capp and Nat Pierce. And they had mics all over the place and it blew your head off. The next night the Count Basie Orchestra led by Grover Mitchell…
